content.text:
A tmux process cannot literally survive a reboot, but `tmux-resurrect` plus `tmux-continuum` can save and reconstruct sessions, windows, panes, layouts, and working directories automatically. [tmux-resurrect documentation](https://github.com/tmux-plugins/tmux-resurrect), [tmux-continuum documentation](https://github.com/tmux-plugins/tmux-continuum).

### 1. Install the plugin manager

```bash
git clone https://github.com/tmux-plugins/tpm ~/.tmux/plugins/tpm
```

Add this near the bottom of `~/.tmux.conf`:

```tmux
set -g status on

set -g @plugin 'tmux-plugins/tpm'
set -g @plugin 'tmux-plugins/tmux-resurrect'
set -g @plugin 'tmux-plugins/tmux-continuum'

set -g @continuum-restore 'on'
set -g @continuum-boot 'on'
set -g @continuum-save-interval '10'

# Optional: restore visible pane history
set -g @resurrect-capture-pane-contents 'on'

# Keep this last
run '~/.tmux/plugins/tpm/tpm'
```

Reload the configuration:

```bash
tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf
```

Then press `Ctrl-b`, followed by uppercase `I`, to install the plugins.

Continuum saves every few minutes and restores when a new tmux server starts. Its boot option generates a user-level systemd service on Linux. [Systemd integration details](https://github.com/tmux-plugins/tmux-continuum/blob/master/docs/systemd_details.md).

### 2. Test saving manually

Inside tmux:

- `Ctrl-b`, then `Ctrl-s` — save
- `Ctrl-b`, then `Ctrl-r` — restore

Verify a save exists:

```bash
ls -l ~/.tmux/resurrect/last
```

Check the generated service:

```bash
systemctl --user status tmux.service
```

### 3. Optional: start tmux before login

For a headless machine where tmux should start immediately at boot:

```bash
sudo loginctl enable-linger "$USER"
```

Lingering starts your user service manager at boot and keeps it running after logout. [systemd loginctl documentation](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/loginctl.html).

This reconstructs the tmux workspace; it does not preserve live in-memory processes across a reboot. Programs such as Codex must be restarted or resumed separately.

*** Add File: docs/PASSENGER_DATA_POLICY.md
+# Passenger Identity Data Policy
+
+Passport numbers and dates of birth are restricted identity data. They are
+collected only to create a booking and must not be reused for analytics,
+marketing, or routine customer-support work.
+
+## Storage and encryption
+
+- The database stores these fields only as versioned AES-256-GCM ciphertext.
+  A fresh 12-byte random IV protects every value, and authenticated context
+  binds each ciphertext to its passenger record and field.
+- `PASSENGER_DATA_ENCRYPTION_KEYS` is a comma-separated key ring in
+  `key-id:base64-key` form. The first key encrypts new values; retained keys
+  decrypt older values during rotation. Every key must be 32 random bytes.
+- Keys must be generated with a cryptographically secure generator and stored
+  in the deployment secret manager, separately from the database. They must
+  never be committed, logged, or baked into an image.
+- A suspected exposure requires an immediate new active key, re-encryption of
+  retained records, revocation of the affected key after old backups age out,
+  and an incident review.
+
+## Access and redaction
+
+- Booking creation is the only normal write path. Plaintext exists only in the
+  request-scoped server process long enough to validate and encrypt it.
+- Customer profiles receive passenger names and travel-assignment fields, but
+  never encrypted or plaintext passport numbers or dates of birth.
+- Routine administration manifests use the same safe projection. Access to an
+  admin route alone is not sufficient to reveal restricted identity data.
+- Booking action results, logs, errors, notifications, analytics, and routine
+  API responses must not contain either plaintext or ciphertext values.
+- Any future operational reveal flow requires a separately authorized,
+  audited, purpose-limited action with step-up staff authentication.
+
+## Retention and deletion
+
+- Restricted identity data expires 30 days after scheduled departure. The
+  application purges expired ciphertext at startup and hourly while retaining
+  non-sensitive booking, passenger, and seat history.
+- A verified customer erasure request can call the server-only
+  `purgePassengerDataForUser` operation immediately. The customer-facing
+  export/deletion workflow remains tracked separately under P5.3.
+- Deleting a booking deletes its passenger rows through the existing database
+  cascade. Database backups follow the deployment backup-retention policy and
+  must age out before a retired decryption key is destroyed.
+- The migration deliberately purges identity values from pre-production demo
+  rows because migration tooling must never receive the runtime encryption
+  key. Bookings and seat assignments remain intact.
+
+## Verification
+
+Automated checks cover authenticated encryption, unique IVs, tamper detection,
+key-ring validation, retention purging, safe view projections, and removal of
+plaintext schema columns. Browser coverage confirms routine staff journeys do
+not expose restricted identity data.

content.text: The interrupted second test was expected from stopping the run mid-flow. I’m inspecting the login form and auth helper now to make the post-login route deterministic for users versus staff.

The app client cannot know the user role from `signIn(..., redirect:false)` alone. I’m going to route normal password-only sign-ins to `/` and route submissions with a staff code to `/staff/mfa`; the staff setup case remains covered because admins without enrollment are redirected by the proxy/layout when they try `/admin` and the E2E helper explicitly expects `/staff/mfa` for setup.

I found the correct fix: after successful credentials sign-in, ask NextAuth for the new session and route from the session flags. That keeps regular users on `/`, sends first-time staff to `/staff/mfa`, and sends verified staff straight to `/admin`.

I’m inspecting the client-address parser and proxy headers; the proxy likely needs to append both forwarded host and forwarded address metadata in the shape the app expects.

The client-address parser is compatible with the proxy’s `X-Forwarded-For`, so I’m narrowing this to the Host header change. NextAuth may not like `Host: localhost:3000` at the app hop while the upstream connection is also port 3000; I’ll inspect any NextAuth errors and then adjust only the forwarded host header Next needs for Server Actions.
